transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Hi, yes, thank you for seeing me. Um, well, I guess I'm here because... well, I'm a secondary school teacher, and over the last couple of years, our district has really pushed us to incorporate a lot of multimedia, you know, recording our lesson videos for the students to access online or review later. And... I just, I can't do it anymore. I can’t stop seeing this... this completely crooked, swollen-looking side of my face on all the lesson videos. 

It's like my jaw and my cheek on that side are just entirely asymmetrical and puffed out, almost distorted. At first, I'd just catch a glimpse of it when I was uploading the files to the portal, but now, I will literally sit at my desk for hours pausing the videos, rewinding them, zooming in, just staring at how deformed I look on camera. 

And the worst part is, once I notice it—which is constantly now—I just feel this overwhelming certainty that the students, the parents who might be watching over their shoulders at home, the other staff members in the building... they must all be staring right at it. There is absolutely no way they are actually listening to anything I'm saying about the curriculum. They're just sitting there looking at this huge, swollen mess of a face. It's gotten to the point where every time I stand at the front of the room or turn on a webcam, I just freeze up because I know that's the only thing anyone is focusing on. I just keep thinking about how distracting and awful it must be for them to have to look at me while I'm trying to teach, and I just... I can't get it out of my head.

When you notice this asymmetry on your face in the videos, do you find yourself doing things like adjusting your camera, changing your posture, or trying to cover part of your face to fix how you look?

Yeah, oh yeah, constantly. It's actually become this whole exhausting routine. Like, before I even think about posting a recorded lesson, or... or even just joining a live Zoom call for a parent-teacher conference, I spend I don't even know how long just messing with the setup. I'll move the webcam up higher, then lower, then I'll try angling it from the left because I think maybe that side doesn't look as puffy, but then the lighting hits it wrong and it looks even worse. So then I'm moving lamps around my home office, trying to wash out the shadows on my cheek. 

And if it's a recorded video... God, it's a nightmare. I'll record a five-minute segment on, you know, the causes of the Civil War or whatever, and then I'll watch it back immediately. And of course, the first thing I see is my jaw looking completely lopsided. So I delete it. I adjust the camera again, I try sitting up straighter, maybe tilting my chin down and to the right, and I record it again. Then I replay that one. And I'll literally sit there replaying tiny clips, like five-second clips, over and over, just watching my mouth move and seeing how deformed that side of my face gets when I talk. 

Sometimes I try to just casually rest my chin in my hand, you know, like I'm just thinking or being expressive, but really I'm just trying to physically cover that swollen part of my cheek so the camera can't see it. But then I think, 'Well, that looks unnatural, they're going to know I'm hiding something.' So I have to scrap that video too. I end up re-recording the exact same lesson so many times... I mean, dozens of times. It takes hours. I'll start at 4 PM and suddenly it's 8 PM and I haven't even finished one short video. Because of it, I'm missing all my actual prep work for the next day, I'm falling behind on grading, and I've even ended up posting the lessons late for my classes, which just makes me feel like a terrible teacher on top of everything else. But I just can't let them see the video if the angle is bad. I just can't.
Can you tell me if it’s mainly the appearance of your face on camera that distresses you, or if it’s more about how others might react or judge you when they see it?

I... gosh, I don't even know if I can separate the two anymore. It’s like they just feed into each other. Because, on the one hand, just seeing it myself makes my stomach drop. I'll be sitting there editing a video, completely alone in my house—my dog is asleep, no one else is around—and I just feel this immense wave of disgust. I look at that swollen, crooked side of my jaw and it’s just so wrong. I can’t stand that it’s my face. Just knowing it looks like that, just seeing the physical proof of it right there on the screen, makes me want to crawl out of my skin, even if I were the last person on earth. 

But then... my brain immediately goes to the students. And the parents. Because if it looks this hideous to me, and I'm just trying to teach a standard lesson, what must they be thinking? High schoolers are brutal, you know? They notice absolutely everything. If a teacher wears the same tie twice in a week, they talk about it. So I just sit there agonizing over the idea of a 15-year-old pausing my video, taking a screenshot of my lopsided face, and sending it to a group chat. The thought of them laughing at it, or even just being repulsed by it... or the parents looking over their shoulders thinking, 'Why does his face look like that? Is there something wrong with him?' 

So I guess... I really don't know which is the main problem. It’s the appearance itself, because it's just so glaringly asymmetrical and horrible to look at, but it's also the absolute certainty that everyone else is judging me for it. I mean, how could they not? If you saw someone with half their face puffed out, you'd stare, right? It's human nature. And as a teacher, I'm literally paid to stand in front of an audience and have them look at me. It's just this constant, exhausting loop. I hate seeing it, and I hate knowing they see it, and I just can't turn off the thoughts about either side of it. It just spirals. Like, even when I'm not on camera, I'll be at the grocery store and I'll catch my reflection in the glass of the freezer aisle, and I'll immediately think about who else in the aisle is looking at me...
Do you experience similar concerns about your appearance in real-life interactions, when you're not on camera or being recorded?

I... gosh, I'm not really sure. I haven't really noticed it being the exact same way when I'm just, you know, existing in a room with people. Like, if I'm just teaching a regular, in-person class without any technology involved... well, it's different, isn't it? Because in the physical classroom—my room is room 204, it's up on the second floor and it has these really large windows on the east side, so the morning light comes in pretty strong and washes everything out anyway—I'm constantly moving. I'm writing on the whiteboard, I'm walking up and down the rows of desks checking on their worksheets, I'm handing out syllabus packets... I'm not just sitting frozen in a little square box on a screen. 

So, because I'm always in motion, I don't have that immediate, undeniable proof staring back at me. I mean, sure, like I said about the grocery store earlier, if I happen to catch my reflection in the glass of the classroom door or a window, I might get a little jolt of panic. I might suddenly remember, 'Oh God, my jaw is swollen, they can see it.' But... I haven't really noticed the same level of absolute, paralyzing obsession in real life. I guess maybe because in person, people are looking at me from all different angles? And high schoolers in a physical room are so distracted anyway. They're trying to sneak looks at their phones under the desks, or they're whispering to their friends, or staring at the clock. 

But on a video... it's just this fixed, two-dimensional image. That lopsided, puffy side of my face is just trapped there, perfectly framed for everyone to scrutinize. There are no distractions. So, no, I don't think it happens the same way in real life. At least, I haven't really felt that same exact, suffocating dread unless there's a camera or a mirror right in front of me. It's mostly just the recordings that completely ruin me, because those are permanent, you know? In person, a moment passes, I turn my head, and it's gone. But a video... a video they can pause. They can rewind it. They can sit there and stare at my cheek for ten minutes if they want to. In real life, I can at least turn my back to them and write on the board to give myself a break, but you can't turn your back on a webcam.
Do you feel significant anxiety or self-consciousness about your appearance when you're interacting with others in person, even outside of teaching or being on camera?

I... well, outside of teaching... I guess I'm just not really sure? I haven't really paid attention to it in the same way, to be completely honest. Like, if I'm just out running errands, say, going to the bank or picking up my dry cleaning. The dry cleaner I go to is this little place over on Elm Street, run by this older couple, and they're always so incredibly busy sorting through the plastic-wrapped racks that they barely even look up when I hand them my ticket. So in situations like that, I don't think I feel that overwhelming panic. Because we're just exchanging pleasantries, you know? It's just, "Here are your shirts, have a good day." It's entirely transactional. I'm moving, they're moving, nobody is really studying anyone else.

And even with friends... I mean, I don't go out a ton lately anyway because I'm always so behind on my grading from all the hours I spend re-recording those video lessons, but... if I do manage to grab a beer with my buddy Mark, for instance, we usually just sit at the bar, right? Not at a booth or a table. So we're sitting side-by-side, facing the bartender or looking up at the TV showing the game. We're not staring directly into each other's faces for hours on end. So I guess... I haven't really noticed it being a huge problem there either. 

I mean, maybe if I were at some formal dinner party where I was forced to sit directly across from someone under a really bright, harsh chandelier for a three-course meal, maybe then I'd start sweating and wondering if they were staring at how puffy my cheek is. But in my normal, day-to-day life outside of the classroom? I just don't know. I haven't really experienced that same level of paralyzing self-consciousness. It’s really just... the camera. Or the mirrors, like I said. But just talking to people? I don't really have a good answer for that, because I just haven't noticed it being a major issue when I'm just trying to live my life off-screen.
Have you ever avoided social situations or felt intense discomfort in face-to-face interactions because of how you think your face looks, even when there’s no camera involved?

I... well, honestly, no. I don't think I've ever outright avoided going somewhere or canceled plans just because of my face, assuming we're just talking about normal, everyday face-to-face stuff. I just haven't noticed that being a thing for me. 

Like, for example, last weekend my sister had a birthday dinner. It was at this Italian place downtown—Luigi's, you know the one? The place with the red checkered tablecloths and the really dim, yellowish lighting, where it's always incredibly loud and packed wall-to-wall with people. I didn't even hesitate to go. I mean, I was completely exhausted because it was the end of the quarter and I had just spent three hours that afternoon trying to edit a bad angle out of my Monday history lecture video, but the thought of not going to the dinner because someone might look at my jaw in person? It just didn't cross my mind. 

Because when I got there, you know, my sister was busy wrangling her two toddlers, my brother-in-law was trying to flag down the waiter for more breadsticks, the people at the table next to us were laughing at some joke... everyone was just so wrapped up in their own little worlds. Nobody was stopping to stare at the puffy side of my face. So I didn't feel any of that intense, crawling-out-of-my-skin discomfort that I get when I'm staring at a recording. I just ate my lasagna and went home. 

I mean, sure, I don't go out to massive parties or huge social events all that often, but that's really just because teaching high school completely drains the life out of you. By Friday at 3:30 PM, after managing 150 teenagers all week and breaking up arguments over who took whose charger, the absolute last thing I want to do is go to a crowded mixer or a loud bar. I just want to go home, feed my dog—he's a golden retriever mix, he has boundless energy and needs a solid walk the second I walk through the door—and just collapse on my couch in sweatpants. 

So if I'm staying in, it's because of fatigue, not because I'm hiding my face from the world. If someone invites me to a backyard barbecue, as long as I know nobody is going to be shoving a smartphone in my face to record a video for social media or whatever, I'm generally perfectly fine to just show up, grab a burger, and talk to people. I don't have that urge to run away and hide from actual, physical people in a room. I just really haven't experienced it like that at all.
When you’re not looking at a camera or a mirror, do you still spend a lot of time thinking about how your face looks, or worrying that others notice something wrong with it?

I mean... well, it all comes back to the videos, really. Even if I'm not physically standing in front of a mirror or actively staring at my webcam in that exact second, my mind is still completely trapped by what's *on* those recordings. 

That’s honestly the whole reason I’m here talking to you today. I'm here because I just cannot stop seeing this crooked, swollen-looking side of my face on my lesson videos. It’s like it’s burned into my retinas. And the worst part is, once I notice it on the screen—which is immediately, the second I hit playback to review the file before I upload it to the school's portal—I just get this sinking, horrible feeling that everyone else is fixated on it, too. 

I mean, I teach 150 kids. That’s 150 students, plus God knows how many parents who are hovering over their shoulders while they do their homework at the kitchen table, and then there's the staff, like the department head who occasionally audits our digital modules to make sure we're hitting the state standards... I just feel like all of them, every single one of them, must be staring at my puffy, lopsided jaw instead of actually listening to a single word I’m saying about the Industrial Revolution or the New Deal. 

So, even when I'm just sitting on my couch miles away from a camera, I'm still agonizing over it, because I know those videos are just sitting there on the server, waiting to be watched. I'll be trying to grade essays at my kitchen table, and all I can think about is some 10th grader pausing the video and taking a screenshot of my cheek to send to their friends in a group chat. It completely takes over my brain because the evidence is just... it's out there, you know? Even if I'm not looking at it right then, I know *they* are looking at it, and it just makes me feel sick to my stomach.
Do you believe that the asymmetry or swelling on the side of your face is something that others would notice and comment on, even though they haven't actually mentioned it to you?

Yeah, well, exactly. That’s... that’s really what I was just trying to say a second ago. Just because they haven't marched up to my desk and said, "Hey, what's wrong with your jaw?" doesn't mean they aren't seeing it. I mean, teenagers are hyper-aware of that kind of stuff, right? They might not say it to my face because I'm the teacher, I'm the one giving them their grades, but you know they're noticing it. 

Like I was just saying, that is the entire reason I made this appointment. I’m here because I absolutely cannot stop seeing this crooked, swollen-looking side of my face every single time I review those lesson videos. It's glaring. And once I notice it—which, again, is instantly—I just know, deep down in my gut, that they have to be seeing it too. I mean, how could they not? The camera is right there. 

So even if a parent hasn't emailed me to ask about it, or the principal hasn't pulled me into his office to ask if I had a bad reaction to a bee sting or something, I just feel like... they must be staring at it. Every time they log into the school portal, the students, their parents, the staff... I just know they're fixated on my face instead of listening to anything I’m saying. It's incredibly frustrating, too, because I put hours into planning these digital modules. I’ll have this whole interactive slide deck prepared for the Cold War, completely color-coded, and I'm sitting there trying to explain the Cuban Missile Crisis, and the whole time I'm recording I'm just thinking, "These 15-year-olds aren't hearing a single word of this." 

They aren't taking notes on the timeline. They're just looking at how lopsided my cheek is. And then I start spiraling, wondering if there's a meme going around the school about it. You know how fast kids can take a screenshot and put some awful caption on it on Snapchat or TikTok? They do it to other teachers all the time for the smallest things. So, yes, I absolutely believe they notice it. The fact that nobody has explicitly commented on it almost makes it worse, honestly, because the silence just lets my imagination fill in the blanks. I just know they're staring at it on those videos, just like I am.
Do you believe that the asymmetry or swelling on the side of your face is a major defect that others should notice, even if they haven't pointed it out to you?

I mean, yes, absolutely. I feel like we're going in circles a bit here, Doctor, because that is exactly what I've been trying to explain this whole time. It's not just some minor, insignificant detail to me, it's... it's a glaring, major defect. 

Like I've been saying, that is the entire reason I'm sitting in this chair right now. I’m here because I just cannot stop seeing this crooked, swollen-looking side of my face on my lesson videos. It's all I can see. And once I notice it—which is the very second the video starts playing, I literally can't look away from it—it just completely takes over. I know, without a shadow of a doubt, that the students, their parents, the staff, whoever is clicking on that link... I just feel like they must be staring at it instead of listening to anything I’m saying. 

How could they not notice it? It’s right there. It’s huge. It takes up half the screen when I'm doing a close-up explanation of a historical document. I'll be trying to break down primary sources for the French Revolution, going into all this detail about the Reign of Terror and Robespierre, and I just know that not a single one of those 150 kids is absorbing a word of it. Because they're just looking at this massive, lopsided swelling on my jaw. 

It completely undermines everything I'm trying to do as an educator. I spend hours, literally hours, making sure these presentations are engaging, making sure the audio is clear, finding the right primary sources so they aren't just reading a boring textbook, and it's all completely ruined by my face. So, yes, even if they aren't raising their hands in a live session or sending me an email to point it out, I know it's a major defect. It's impossible to miss. I just know they see it exactly the way I do.
Do you believe that the asymmetry or swelling on the side of your face is caused by an actual physical or medical problem?

I mean... I don't really know. I honestly don't. I guess I haven't really thought about it like... like a disease or a specific medical condition, you know? I haven't gone to a regular doctor or a dentist to ask if it's, I don't know, a swollen lymph node or some kind of weird bone growth or an allergic reaction. 

I mean, sure, sometimes when I'm lying in bed at 2 AM and I can't sleep because I'm dreading recording the next day's module, I'll pull out my phone and go down these massive internet rabbit holes. I'll be on WebMD reading about salivary gland issues or asymmetrical muscle development or whatever, just trying to find some logical explanation for why my face looks like this. But I don't actually *know* if it's a medical problem. I don't have any proof of that. 

And honestly, Doctor, it almost doesn't even matter to me *why* it's happening, because the end result is exactly the same. Whether it's some undiagnosed physical issue or just my face completely betraying me at 32 years old, it's still right there on the screen. It doesn't change the fact that it looks awful. Like, if a doctor told me tomorrow, "Oh, it's just a harmless cyst" or "It's just the way your jaw is settling," that wouldn't make me feel any better. It wouldn't change the fact that my entire sophomore history class is still staring at this huge, lopsided puffiness while I'm trying to explain the economic impacts of the Great Depression. 

So, no, I don't have some specific medical theory about what's causing it underneath the skin. I just know what it looks like on the outside. I just know it's there, and it's completely derailing my career, and I can't stop seeing it every single time I turn on that webcam.
Outside of your concerns about your appearance on camera, have you experienced significant distress or difficulties in your daily life because of how you think your face looks?

Oh, God, yes. It’s... it’s bleeding into absolutely everything. It’s not just the camera thing, it’s my entire life right now. I mean, I’ve completely fallen behind on my lesson planning, which is huge for me because I used to be the guy who had his whole semester mapped out by August. I take a lot of pride in my curriculum. But now? I can’t focus. I sit down at my desk to grade essays or build out the next unit, and instead, I’m just paralyzed. I’m obsessing over my jaw, taking pictures on my phone in different lighting to see how bad the swelling looks, and before I know it, three hours have gone by and so much of my work just never gets finished on time anymore. 

And it’s not just the classroom stuff, either. It's the extra-curriculars, which are honestly the parts of the job I usually love the most. I’m supposed to be mentoring a group of at-risk sophomores, and I coach the boys' basketball team. Well, assistant coach, but still, it's a big time commitment. But lately, I’ve been missing practices. I’ll just sit in my office with the door locked, avoiding everyone, because I can't bear the thought of standing in that bright gymnasium overhead lighting where everyone can see my face from every possible angle. I’ve left the head coach hanging so many times, and I’ve completely ghosted my mentoring kids during our scheduled blocks. 

It’s gotten so bad that the administrators have actually started a paper trail. That's how bad it is. They’re formally documenting all my missed deadlines, the times I didn't submit my lesson plans to the shared drive, and all the coverage problems I’m causing. Because when I don't show up for cafeteria duty or I can't bring myself to leave my office for a live class, they have to pull other teachers on their prep periods to watch my kids. It's humiliating to know your colleagues are picking up your slack. I had a sit-down with the vice principal last week, and seeing that file... the actual physical file of all my screw-ups... I’m genuinely terrified. I’m terrified that I’m really, really close to losing my position. Teaching, coaching, being there for these kids... it's my whole identity. But I just can't function normally right now. I can't just walk out there and pretend everything is fine when my face looks like this.
Outside of your concerns about your face, do you find yourself frequently worried about other physical symptoms or body parts, even if doctors haven’t found anything wrong?

No, not at all. I mean... I really don't. It's just the face. Honestly, I don't even think I have the mental bandwidth to worry about anything else right now, even if something *was* wrong. Like, if I woke up tomorrow and my knee was killing me, or if I had some weird ache in my stomach, I don't think I'd even care. I really wouldn't. Because it's all... it's just all focused right here on my jaw. 

I used to be pretty in tune with my body, you know? Like I said, I help coach the basketball team, so I used to run a few miles a week, lift weights a little bit in the school weight room after hours just to stay in shape so I could actually keep up with the boys during drills. If I pulled a muscle back then, I'd notice it. But now? I don't care about my fitness, I don't care if I'm out of shape, I don't care about any other part of my appearance or my health. It's like the rest of me doesn't even exist anymore. 

When I look in the mirror—which I do constantly, even when I tell myself I'm going to stop, I just end up back in the bathroom staring at the glass—I don't even see my shoulders or my chest or my hair. My eyes just immediately, automatically lock onto that swelling on the side of my face. It's like a magnet. I can't look at anything else. 

So, no, I'm definitely not sitting around worrying that I have heart problems or, I don't know, a bad back or some other physical defect. None of that matters to me. If somebody told me today that I had a completely torn meniscus and needed surgery, I'd be like, "Fine, whatever, take the knee, just please fix my face." Because my knee isn't what's on camera. My knee isn't what my students are staring at when I'm trying to teach. It’s this one, massive, glaring issue on my face that’s ruining my life. Everything else is completely fine, or at least, I wouldn't even notice if it wasn't, because this one thing just takes up absolutely all the space in my brain.
Do you believe that the asymmetry or swelling you see on your face is something that most people would barely notice, or do you feel like it's much more obvious than it actually is?

Barely notice? No... no, I don't think that at all. I mean, how could they barely notice it? It feels... it feels like there's a giant spotlight on it. That's actually exactly why I'm here, why I finally agreed to talk to someone, because... well, it really all comes back to those lesson videos. We have to record everything for the digital portal, right? And when I sit down to review the footage—which I'm supposed to do just to check the audio levels, make sure the slides are syncing up, just normal teacher stuff—I absolutely can’t stop seeing it. 

It’s just right there, this crooked, swollen-looking side of my face, just dominating the little webcam box in the corner of the screen. It’s literally all I can look at. And my thought process is, if it’s all *I* can look at, how could anyone else possibly ignore it? Once I notice it on the playback, which is immediately, I just get this horrible, sinking feeling in the pit of my stomach. Because I know... I just know that the students, and the parents who are walking around in the kitchen behind them while their kids are on their laptops, and the administrative staff who randomly audit our digital classrooms... I feel like they must all just be staring right at it. 

How could they not? It's so glaring. I'll be in the middle of giving this really detailed, passionate lecture, trying to be an engaging educator, and the whole time I just have this overwhelming certainty that no one is listening to a single word I’m saying. They aren't hearing the lesson. They aren't taking notes. They're just staring at my face, looking at how lopsided and puffy it is, probably texting each other about it or wondering what the hell is wrong with Mr. Davis. So, no, I definitely don't think it's something people barely notice. I feel like it's the absolute only thing they notice about me now.
Do you believe that the asymmetry or swelling on your face is something that most people would consider a serious or obvious defect, even though they may not mention it to you?

A serious defect? I mean... I don't know if that's the exact phrase they're using in their heads. Like, I have no idea if my students or the other teachers are looking at me and thinking, 'Oh, Mr. Davis has a serious medical defect.' I really couldn't tell you what label they put on it. But... but as for it being obvious? Yeah. I mean, like I just said, it’s... it’s glaring. It’s completely impossible to miss. 

But the part about them not mentioning it... God, that’s honestly the worst part of all of this. It’s the silence. Because nobody says a word. Not a single person has ever come up to me and said, 'Hey, what's going on with your jaw?' or 'Did you get your wisdom teeth out?' And you'd think, logically, that would make me feel better, right? Like, oh, they aren't saying anything, so maybe it's not that bad. But it does the exact opposite. It's like... it's this massive, suffocating elephant in the room. 

I'll be in the staff lounge, right? Just standing by the copier, trying to get my worksheets printed, and Brenda from the English department will come over to talk to me about the new standardized testing schedule. And she's making eye contact, she's smiling, but her eyes... they do this little darting thing. Just a fraction of a second, down to the side of my face, and then right back up to my eyes. And she doesn't say a word about it. She just keeps talking about rubrics and state standards like everything is completely normal. And the whole time, I'm just standing there sweating, my heart is pounding out of my chest, because I know she sees it. I know she's trying so incredibly hard to be polite and pretend she doesn't notice this huge, puffy, lopsided mess on my face. 

It's the politeness that absolutely kills me. And the kids do it too, which is how I really know it's bad. I mean, teenagers are usually ruthless, you know? If you wear a weird tie or get a bad haircut, they will roast you for forty-five minutes straight, they have absolutely no filter. But with this... it's like it's so bad, so obviously wrong, that even the sophomores don't want to touch it. They just stare at the webcam or stare at me in the hall, and they stay totally quiet. So... yeah, I don't know if they consider it a 'serious defect' or whatever. I don't know what they call it. I just know that everyone is tiptoeing around it, and that just proves to me how terrible it actually is.
Do you believe that the way your face looks is something that sets you apart from others in a very negative way, or do you think others might have similar concerns about their own appearance?

I mean... sure, I guess on some level, everyone has things they don't love about themselves, right? Like, I teach high school, so I see teenagers freaking out over a pimple on picture day, or worrying about if their clothes are cool enough. And even the other teachers—like Jim in the math department, he’s always making self-deprecating jokes about losing his hair. But... no. No, this is entirely different. What I'm dealing with absolutely sets me apart in the most negative, isolating way possible. It makes me feel like I'm living on a completely different planet from everyone else. 

Jim can make a joke about his hairline and then just go right back to teaching calculus. He doesn't think about it again. But for me... I mean, that’s exactly what I was trying to explain about the videos a minute ago. It’s literally the entire reason I’m here in your office today. I’m here because I just absolutely can’t stop seeing this crooked, swollen-looking side of my face on the lesson videos. It's not just a passing thought. It completely consumes me. I will literally sit at my desk at home for three hours trying to edit a forty-five-minute lecture. Three hours! Just pausing, rewinding, staring at the screen, looking at how deformed my jaw looks under the desk lamp, trying to figure out if there's any possible angle where it doesn't look like a total monstrosity. 

And once I notice it—which is the second I hit play—the panic just sets in. Because I know that if it's this obvious to me, it's obvious to everyone. I just get this overwhelming, paralyzing feeling that the students, their parents who might be walking through the room behind them, the administrative staff who check the portal... they must all just be staring at it instead of listening to a single word I’m saying. I put so much work into my lesson plans, you know? I try to make history engaging for these kids, I really do. But it feels completely pointless. Because I’m sitting there talking about the Industrial Revolution, and I just know, deep down in my bones, that nobody is hearing a word of it. They’re just fixated on my face. 

So, no, I don't think other people have concerns like this. Normal people don't feel like their face is a distraction to the general public. They don't feel like a walking freak show that ruins their own career. It completely separates me from normal society, it really does.
